1755071375377875436 [2024-02-07] @QiaochuYuan 💜 49 🔁 1
thinking about the long tweet meta. first, it’s a waste to write a tweet that’s only *slightly* long. people have to click an extra time to read the rest of a long tweet past the first 280 chars. so the game is to invite people to make the click

so the first 280 chars should be a good advertisement for the rest of the long tweet; it should promise the reader that something interesting is waiting, and then the rest of the long tweet should deliver on that promise. so no 300 character tweets unless somehow the last 20 characters are an amazing punchline; that’s not worth the extra click to your readers

second, a question any long tweet has to answer is: why isn’t this a thread? i personally have really enjoyed learning how to write threads well, it’s a distinct form of writing with its own distinct advantages. the key fact about threads, which i was introduced to by @visakanv’s twitter_rpg_strategy_guide.txt, is that any individual tweet in a thread can be RT’d or QT’d, by anyone, including yourself. (also that any individual tweet can itself be a QT!) 

what this means is that it’s worth learning how to write threads in such a way that every individual tweet stands somewhat on its own, and makes sense and says something comprehensible even when RT’d / QT’d outside the context of the rest of the thread. ideally (imo) each tweet in a thread should make exactly one point or introduce exactly one new idea - they get very cluttered if you try to say too much at once. the thread as a whole serves as a journey through the individual ideas or points in each tweet, and can also offer detours via QTs to other threads. one of the cool things learning how to thread like this does is that you can be surprised by which tweets in a thread resonate with other people - maybe you had a grand conclusion but it’s a throwaway tweet in the middle that people actually RT and QT and reply to. this is a level of granularity of feedback on your writing and ideas that longform doesn’t support by default (although google doc comments can be even more granular, eg) and i’ve learned a lot from it

from this perspective long tweets offer a return back to longform, but somewhat more casual longform than eg a ‘stack post. sometimes you wanna describe an idea that takes longer than 280 chars to meaningfully express. sometimes you wanna ramble and think out loud in a less structured way than a thread (this is what i’m doing rn). threads also have the disadvantage that if you do too good a job making the individual tweets stand alone then when they get RT’d and QT’d they may not even look like part of a thread, so people may not even click through to the rest of it. long tweets have the advantage (and disadvantage) that the whole thing is RT’d or QT’d at once, meaning it’s harder to single out individual bits but the whole package gets transported around twitter together, and unlike an external link it’s all still happening on twitter. typically when i write long threads the first tweet gets RT’d and QT’d the most and all the numbers drop off from there. so i’m interested in the ability of long tweets to preserve what might otherwise be a chopped-up thread as more of an organic whole. anyway that’s what i’ve got so far, time to get some food now. thanks for reading

rating.reasoning_summary: This strand represents a multi-year intellectual project centered on Visa's 2019 'disagreement diagram' as a boundary object for understanding how different life experiences produce different conclusions. The arc moves from Visa's initial articulation of 'vision-based disagreement' through practical conversational techniques (tactical agreement, asking questions), to broader applications in conflict resolution, storytelling, and community building. The discourse is primarily constructive rather than dialectical—people building on and applying the core insight rather than challenging it. The diagram itself becomes a memetic artifact that gets quoted/shared across years (2019-2025), with participants like Malcolm Ocean, Tasshin, Rich Decibels, and others extending it into domains like cult offramps, embodiment debates, and interpersonal mediation. The strand shows high cohesion (recurring cast returning to the same framework) and medium-high utility (practical conversational tools), but evolution is somewhat limited—the core insight remains static while applications multiply.

essential_tweets.annotation: The Origin: Visa's first articulation of the core principle—disagreements require identifying assumptions and discussing experiences
The Viral Moment: The diagram tweet that becomes the recurring boundary object, asking 'how have your experiences been different?'
The Playbook: Visa explicitly constructs the conversational technique—ask about experiences and assumptions, not conclusions
Ultimape's Extension: Applying the framework to memetic theory and 'alternative models of reality' as a game
Conflict Resolution Application: Visa uses the framework to address trauma/abuse language barriers in public discourse
Domestic Application: Visa reveals using diagrams/maps with his wife for relationship alignment, making the abstract concrete
The MDMA Hypothesis: JD Pressman suggests drugs help people 'blurt out what they're actually thinking'—a chemical shortcut to the diagram
Malcolm Ocean's Synthesis: Connecting the framework to 'offramps for cults' and memetic mediation projects
Rich Decibels' Restatement: 'People who disagree aren't wrong—they have different experiences and values' (152 likes, independent validation)
2024 Reaffirmation: Visa returns to the diagram 5 years later, noting people fight 'without ever clarifying their terms'—the problem persists

rating.reasoning_summary: This strand traces the multi-year evolution of a psychological/somatic concept anchored by RomeoStevens76's 'Ice Cream Probability Shape' tweet (2021). The boundary object is the metaphor of childhood conditioning creating lifelong muscle tension patterns. The discourse is primarily constructive—practitioners of Alexander Technique, somatic therapies, and contemplative practice use the tweet as a shared reference point to explore how early conditioning manifests as physical tension, and how to release it. The arc moves from initial recognition (Qiaochu's 2019 pre-context on school conditioning) through Romeo's crystallization, into practical applications (Rich's TRE/MDMA experiments, Yatharth's 'Walmart problem'), and finally theoretical synthesis (Johnsonmxe's vasomuscular computation model). The strand demonstrates high evolution—from abstract critique to embodied practice to mechanistic theory—and high utility for both the contemplative community and outsiders seeking to understand psychosomatic patterns.

The boundary object is the original tweet itself, which becomes a recurring meme/reference point. The arc is *iterative rather than evolutionary*—the community repeatedly returns to this idea across 5+ years, applying it to new contexts (unemployment-cortisol hypothesis, sex positivity discourse, Buddhist saints, rationalist orgy culture). It's more of a 'sustained riff' than a dialectical refinement, though it does spawn useful sub-concepts like 'treehouse energy' and 'surreal unbotheredness.' High cohesion (same core users), medium utility (provides vocabulary for a real phenomenon but doesn't build new frameworks).
